title: ‘How the F— Would You Get This Movie Made in America?’ Christine Vachon, Film4, BBC Film Put ‘Trainspotting,’ ‘Ratcatcher’ and ‘The Wicker Man’ Through the 2026 Greenlight Test
description: Would “Trainspotting” get financed today? Could Lynne Ramsay survive the jump from shorts to a first feature? And might “The Wicker Man,” once treat
body:
Would “Trainspotting” get financed today? Could Lynne Ramsay survive the jump from shorts to a first feature? And might “The Wicker Man,” once treated as a problem child, now look like exactly the kind of genre package buyers chase?

	That was the conceit of a lively session hosted by Wendy Mitchell, with Picturehouse’s creative director Clare Binns, Killer Films’ Christine Vachon, Film4’s head of distribution and sales Stefanie Fahrion, BBC Film’s commissioning executive Alice Ojha and Casarotto’s Simon Renshaw asked to assess British classics as if they had just landed on their desks in 2026.
	

	Nobody suggested the market had become kinder, but several films looked less risky than their loglines might suggest.

	
		The Talking Factor	

	First up was “Trainspotting”: heroin use, a dead baby, filthy toilets, heavy Scottish dialect and no obvious box-office cast.

	Binns immediately went to Danny Boyle’s previous film, calling “Shallow Grave” “one of the most exciting films I ever saw” and saying it announced “a new voice.” Fahrion saw upside in the extremity. The film had “so many iconic moments,” she said, with enough “shock value” to create a “talking factor” and “FOMO” around scenes audiences felt they had to see, and today would likely virally share. Renshaw called it “a big swing,” but also “something that’s going to get people talking.” Vachon was less concerned still. “I pitch it as genre or genre adjacent,” she said. At the right price, “I don’t think it’s risky at all.”
	
		Soft Money, Then Sell	

	Structure was the focus for Bill Forsyth’s feel good “Local Hero.” “I don’t think you get any American equity or a pre-buy unless it was a really big, big star,” said Vachon. Better, she argued, to make it “with as much soft money as possible” and then sell it for “a nice high price to the U.S.”
	

	Binns saw an audience play. Older cinemagoers remain underserved, she said. “They might not come opening weekend,” but “this will be a word of mouth” film.
	
		First Features: Still the Hurdle	

	Ramsay’s “Ratcatcher” brought the financing gap into sharper focus.

	Renshaw called “that leap from shorts to that first feature” the hurdle, with known cast often crucial in getting financiers and distributors comfortable.

	This is where, in the U.K. at least, public backing can enter. Fahrion noted that voices as unique and challenging as Ramsay’s often originate with public development or production money.

	Vachon’s U.S. take was starker. “What is this public funding of which you speak?” she joked, before proposing another panel title: “How the fuck would you get this movie made in America?”

	Her answer: “We’d make it for about $300,000.” The job, she said, is to ask: “How do we create a case for this?”
	
		Genre Looks Safer	

	Then came “The Wicker Man”: paganism, full frontal nudity, a remote island and human sacrifice.

	Vachon called it “exactly what… the A24s, Neons, etc. are looking for right now.” Renshaw noted it could be made inexpensively, while Binns saw a hook in casting an actor, in that classics case Richard Chamberlain, “doing something new, different for him.” 

	How times change: when released British Lion packaged it as the secondary feature to “Don’t Look Now.” 

	And the worst pitch Renshaw ever received?

	“’The Sixth Sense,’ but it’s a dog.”

schema.headline: ‘How the F— Would You Get This Movie Made in America?’ Christine Vachon, Film4, BBC Film Put ‘Trainspotting,’ ‘Ratcatcher’ and ‘The Wicker Man’ Through the 2026 Greenlight Test

title: ‘The State of Us’ Review: A Pair of Spirited Performances Lift a Familiar Yorkshire Tearjerker
description: The weather being what it is in Yorkshire, a sunroof is not a top priority for most car buyers in that English county — but the tired hatchback driv
body:
The weather being what it is in Yorkshire, a sunroof is not a top priority for most car buyers in that English county — but the tired hatchback driven by young slacker Frankie (Samuel Bottomley) has one. That’s the first of a few improbabilities in “The State of Us,” an occasionally hokey but winningly sweet-natured buddy comedy from British newcomer Ollie Gardner and Jake Harvey, and it’s a forgivable one: How else, at a key emotional juncture, will his ailing best friend Taylor (Callum Scott Howells) stand up in the car to freely embrace the cold night with arms outstretched? It’s a shameless cliché of an image, recycled from the likes of “The Perks of Being a Wallflower” and TV’s “Euphoria,” but the film gets away with the steal, in large part because Frankie and Taylor are, at least for a moment, chasing the life they’ve seen in slicker American youth movies.
	

	The life they actually live, meanwhile, mixes grainily downbeat British social realism of the Paul Laverty-scripted Ken Loach school with flashes of more Hollywoodized sentimentality and narrative contrivance — as Taylor, a terminally cancer-stricken young man living in a hospice, is broken out of his glum surroundings by Frankie, his irresponsible bestie, cuing one wild night of boyish misbehavior and more mature emotional reckonings. 


	The result isn’t always convincing, but it’s far more consistently likable, thanks in large part to lively performances by Howells (TV’s “It’s a Sin”) and especially Bottomley (“How to Have Sex”), who maintain a key sense of hard-times kinship and tension in the bond at the film’s center. Premiering in the main competition at Edinburgh, “The State of Us” should continue to please crowds at smaller festivals; theatrical prospects are modest, but streaming and broadcast potential is strong.
	

	A brief prologue outlines the childhood damage still borne by boisterous ne’er-do-well Frankie, who lost his mother at an early age, and whose incapable father left him to be raised in Taylor’s more stable household; already best buds, the boys wound up closer to brothers. When we cut to the present day, however, it’s clear something unspecified has gone awry in this chosen-family setup. The friends haven’t seen each other in some time, though Frankie spends many an evening parked outside the hospice in his car, summoning the gumption to visit. When he does, it’s after hours: Breaking into the building via an elderly patient’s window, he ropes a bewildered Taylor into his late-night escape plan without so much as a friendly catch-up. 

	His rashness may be ill-advised, but it does abet the film’s fleet pacing: Cut to a brisk 90 minutes by ace editor Chris Gill (“Kneecap,” “28 Days Later”) and Abi Wright, “The State of Us” ably swings between tragedy and farce in the course of its overnight structure, even making more-or-less sense of an awkwardly shoehorned romantic subplot between Taylor and enigmatic cool girl Rosie (Safia Oakley-Green, the gifted star of indie horror “Out of Darkness,” making the most of a stock role), whom he meets at the scuzzy house party Frankie insists on crashing, and with whom he has more in common than meets the eye. 

	The extended party setpiece allows for some amusing scatological hijinks, but the film is most moving and enjoyable when simply focused on its two leads, whether talking things out in the car or on the country hill of sundry childhood memories. (“The Outrun” DP Yunus Roy Imer keeps the shooting intimate and unfussy, but the rolling beauty of the Yorkshire landscape offers some valuable background support.) Howells, gifted the more openly sympathetic role, puts his naturally anxious brows and forlorn demeanor to good use as Taylor, without making him too much of a victim; there are glimpses here of the buoyant, nurturing partner that he used to be in the friendship. 

	But it’s Bottomley who impresses most here, at every turn lining Frankie’s obnoxious, juvenile antics with soulful self-doubt, and terror of yet more grief crashing his still-young life. As “The State of Us” unsubtly but effectively turns on the waterworks, it’s him, as much as his dying friend, we find ourselves dabbing our eyes for. He, too, has earned some time out of the sunroof.

schema.headline: ‘The State of Us’ Review: A Pair of Spirited Performances Lift a Familiar Yorkshire Tearjerker

title: Selena Gomez Slams ‘Completely Meritless’ Wondermind Lawsuit, Will File to Dismiss ‘Baseless Claims’
description: Selena Gomez and her legal team have released a fiery statement after the “Only Murders in the Building” star was accused of defrauding investors in
body:
Selena Gomez and her legal team have released a fiery statement after the “Only Murders in the Building” star was accused of defrauding investors in her mental health startup, Wondermind, in a federal lawsuit filed Thursday. 

	“The allegations that Selena Gomez engaged in any way whatsoever in any purported ‘fraud’ or other wrongdoing are completely meritless, both factually and legally,” Gomez’s litigator, Mathew S. Rosengart, told People. “We will vigorously defend these false allegations and indeed are filing a motion to dismiss the baseless claims against her.”
	

	According to The New York Times, the lawsuit, which also names Gomez’s mother and Wondermind co-founder Mandy Teefey as a defendant, claims the Wondermind team “falsely represented” the trajectory and leadership structure of the media company, which was founded in 2021 as a way to make mental health resources more accessible. Investors claimed that Gomez and her mother solicited about $1.2 million from them.


	The suit alleges that Gomez had signed a contract stating that she would be “actively building the company as its head of marketing,” but has since “ignored” the agreement. It also claims that there were said to be partnerships with Fidelity and J.P. Morgan that would allow Wondermind to provide mental health services to their employees, but they “did not exist.” Celebrity profiles, a “groundbreaking app” and advertising deals that were promised also fell through, the lawsuit states.

	The lawsuit also says that Wondermind “quietly collapsed around them,” while “not one of its founders, officers, or directors said a word to the investors.” Investors claim they only found out about the “utter financial and operational disarray at Wondermind” from a 2025 story published by The Cut. The exposé alleged that Gomez was trying to distance herself from the company and outlined the messy firing of chief executive Daniella Pierson.
	

	Teefey has yet to comment on the suit, but Pierson told The New York Times that she “categorically denies the allegations against her and welcomes the opportunity to present concrete documentation and financial records that establish the facts.”

schema.headline: Selena Gomez Slams ‘Completely Meritless’ Wondermind Lawsuit, Will File to Dismiss ‘Baseless Claims’

title: Adam Scott Says His Daughter’s Acting Class Was Forced to Watch His Failed ‘Office’ Audition as an Example of What Not to Do
description: Once upon a time, “Severance” star Adam Scott auditioned for the beloved sitcom “The Office.” Years later, he’s reliving the memories of that failed
body:
Once upon a time, “Severance” star Adam Scott auditioned for the beloved sitcom “The Office.” Years later, he’s reliving the memories of that failed audition after his daughter’s acting teacher had the class compare Scott’s audition tape to John Krasinski’s successful tape.

	“He put it to the class like, ‘Okay. Let’s discuss why he got the job, and he didn’t,'” Scott said on Thursday’s episode of “The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon.”
	

	“But I’m just happy to know that in a prestigious acting class, I’m the subject of what not to do,” Scott continued.


	“She was mortified,” Scott said of his daughter’s reaction. “And when she was walking out, the teacher stopped her, he’s like, ‘Hey, um, do you know one of them? Like, what…’ and then he kind of put two and two together with her last name and he felt terrible.”

	After auditioning, Krasinski was ultimately cast as Jim Halpert on the NBC series that ran from 2005 to 2013. Scott did go on to star in a sitcom of his own, “Parks and Recreation,” which ran from 2009 to 2015 and starred Amy Poehler, Rashida Jones and Aubrey Plaza.

	Elsewhere on “The Tonight Show,” Scott fielded questions about “Severance” Season 3, which is currently in production in New York, and said he doesn’t know when it will release. He is starring alongside Robert De Niro in the new movie “The Whisper Man,” which releases Aug. 28 on Netflix.

	After his breakout role on “The Office,” Krasinski went on to direct and star in “A Quiet Place.”

schema.headline: Adam Scott Says His Daughter’s Acting Class Was Forced to Watch His Failed ‘Office’ Audition as an Example of What Not to Do

title: Locarno: Marco Cavazzin’s ‘Mutrion,’ Set in the Venice Lagoon, Scoops Leopards of Tomorrow Director Award
description: “Mutrion,” a short film set in the Venice lagoon by 26-year-old Italian director Marco Cavazzin, has scooped the best director award at the Locarno
body:
“Mutrion,” a short film set in the Venice lagoon by 26-year-old Italian director Marco Cavazzin, has scooped the best director award at the Locarno Film Festival’s Pardi di Domani (Leopards of Tomorrow) section.

	“Mutrion,” which is the only Italian entry in the section, stars Manfredi Marini, who previously starred in Giovanni Tortorici’s “Nineteen,” and Giulio Maroncelli and is produced by the independent studio Etimo. The short, shot entirely on the lagoon islands, is supported by the Veneto Film Commission and  distributed by Italy’s Cattive Produzioni.
	

	“In a lagoon suspended in time, legend has it that sooner or later every inhabitant loses the toenail of their right big toe,” says the synopsis. “It has never happened to Marco. But now that he has returned, something inside him is beginning to crack.” 


	The story follows Marco (played by Manfredi Marini), who in childhood was nicknamed “Mutrion” (which means “sulky”). Marco left the lagoon area at age twenty. Unlike the other locals, he never lost his toenail. Returning four years later, he faces the community’s tacit expectations and structural isolation, causing something deep within him to fracture as the landscape shifts between physical reality and psychological projection.

	“This short stems from the desire to tell a story of return, the attempt to reconnect with a place that has become both familiar and distant over time. In the Venetian lagoon, rituals, superstitions and family stories are still present and continue to shape collective identity,” Cavazzin said in his directors’ statement.
	

	Locarno’s Leopards of Tomorrow selection was judged by a jury panel made up by Lebanese director Mounia Akl; South African producer Steven Markovitz and Italian director Antonio Piazza. Mutrion was the only Italian entry among 20 works from all over the world, including France, the U.K., Iran, Qatar, China, Taiwan, the U.S. and Ukraine.

schema.headline: Locarno: Marco Cavazzin’s ‘Mutrion,’ Set in the Venice Lagoon, Scoops Leopards of Tomorrow Director Award

title: Dave Marsh, Bruce Springsteen Biographer and Rock Critic, Dies at 76
description: Dave Marsh, the music critic and biographer who documented the early days of Bruce Springsteen in his influential 1979 book “Born to Run,” died Frid
body:
Dave Marsh, the music critic and biographer who documented the early days of Bruce Springsteen in his influential 1979 book “Born to Run,” died Friday in his Connecticut home. He was 76.

	Jim Rotolo, who hosts the Springsteen-fan cast “The Wild & The Innocent” on SiriusXM, confirmed Marsh’s death in a Facebook post on Saturday morning.

	“Dave wrote several books about Bruce as part of a remarkable body of work spanning some 25 titles,” Rotolo wrote, along with a picture of himself, Springsteen and Marsh. “A longtime rock critic for Creem and Rolling Stone, he was also one of the creators of ‘E Street Radio’ and hosted ‘Kick Out the Jams’ on SiriusXM for 19 years. Rest easy, Dave. Thank you for everything, my friend. You will be missed.”
	

	“Born to Run: The Bruce Springsteen Story” was one of the first extensive biographies written about the Boss, who was still rising through his young career when it was published in 1979. “Born to Run” followed Springsteen’s journey from local New Jersey rocker to budding global phenomenon and shared a name with Springsteen’s 1975 breakout album.

	Marsh, who penned several works about Springsteen, also published texts on the Who, Sly & the Family Stone, the Beatles, Creedence Clearwater Revival and Black Sabbath. He was also one of the earliest editors of Creem magazine and was a frequent contributor to Rolling Stone.

	In 2004, Marsh launched the “Kick Out the James” radio show, which he hosted for almost two decades. He also co-created “E Street Radio” for the broadcaster.
	

	Marsh’s daughter, Kristen Ann Carr, died in 1993 at 21 years old from sarcoma, a rare form of cancer that affects bones and muscle tissue. In his daughter’s honor, Marsh founded the Kristen Ann Carr Fund to help families of cancer patients and to advance research for sarcoma treatment.

	Marsh is survived by his wife, Barbara Carr.

schema.headline: Dave Marsh, Bruce Springsteen Biographer and Rock Critic, Dies at 76

title: Nate Bargatze Sets Guinness World Record for Most Tickets Sold for a Stand-Up Comedy Tour (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
Nate Bargatze and his “Big Dumb Eyes” just set a Guinness World Record.

	The Tennessee-born comedian has officially sold the most tickets for a sta
body:
Nate Bargatze and his “Big Dumb Eyes” just set a Guinness World Record.

	The Tennessee-born comedian has officially sold the most tickets for a stand-up comedy tour, surpassing the previously record held by Jeff Dunham.

	Bargatze will be presented with the Guinness World Record onstage at the Scotiabank Arena in Toronto on Saturday. Ahead of the show, his “Big Dumb Eyes” world tour had sold approximately 2,016,254 tickets, passing Dunham’s “Spark of Insanity” tour, which sold 1,981,720 tickets. The final ticket number on Bargatze’s Guinness World Records certificate will be confirmed later this weekend.
	

	Bargatze accomplished the feat at an impressive pace. To achieve the previous record, Dunham sold 1,981,720 tickets across 386 venues between Sept. 13, 2007, and Aug. 21, 2010 (35 months and 8 days). Bargatze’s “Big Dumb Eyes” tour, which began on April 6, 2025, crossed the 2 million mark after just 16 months and 10 days — and across only 128 venues. (There were also no puppets on the Bargatze tour.)


	Along the way, Bargatze broke 84 venue records, according to his reps, which included becoming the only comedian to sell out three consecutive performances at Nashville’s Bridgestone Arena in a single calendar year — a feat matched only by Taylor Swift and Garth Brooks.

	Bargatze, whose clean, deadpan comedy has made him famous among all age groups, was crowned by Pollstar as the highest-grossing stand-up comic, with $77.5 million reported in 2025 alone. Earlier this year, he crossed over onto the silver screen with his movie “The Breadwinner,” and he is currently planning to build a $350 million theme park in his home state of Tennessee called Nateland.
	

	Bargatze is repped by Brillstein Entertainment Partners, UTA, Ginsburg Daniels Kallis and 2PM Sharp.

schema.headline: Nate Bargatze Sets Guinness World Record for Most Tickets Sold for a Stand-Up Comedy Tour (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Box Office: ‘The End of Oak Street’ Chomps on $8.1 Million, But ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Is Still No. 1 With $19 Million
description:
“Spider-Man: Brand New Day” led the box office again on Friday despite competition from Anne Hathaway and a horde of hungry dinosaurs.

	The Warner
body:
“Spider-Man: Brand New Day” led the box office again on Friday despite competition from Anne Hathaway and a horde of hungry dinosaurs.

	The Warner Bros. sci-fi thriller “The End of Oak Street” landed in second place on opening day with $8.1 million from 3,446 North American theaters. Rivals estimate the film will earn about $18.7 million domestically by Sunday. That’s a soft start since “Oak Street” cost more than $80 million to produce. Reviews (84% on Rotten Tomatoes) and word-of-mouth (”B” grade on CinemaScore exit polls) have been positive, so there is a chance “Oak Street” sticks around in theaters and justifies its price tag.
	

	“It Follows” filmmaker David Robert Mitchell wrote and directed “The End of Oak Street,” which chronicles a suburban family whose neighborhood is suddenly blipped to prehistoric times. Hathaway stars alongside Ewan McGregor, Maisy Stella, Christian Convery and Jordan Alexa Davis.


	This weekend’s other major newcomer, “PAW Patrol: The Dino Movie,” took third after earning $7.35 million on Friday from 3,545 North American cinemas. The animated family adventure should dig up about $20 million for Paramount through the weekend. That projection aligns with its predecessor, “The Mighty Movie,” which opened with $22 million and grossed $205 million by the end of its run.

	“Spider-Man: Brand New Day” still reigned supreme with $19 million domestically on Friday. Through its third weekend, the Marvel-Sony tentpole is targeting $67 million, which represents about a 53% decline from last week’s numbers. That would push “Brand New Day’s” North American revenues to roughly $783 million.
	

	Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” is still holding strong at No. 4 through its fifth weekend. The Greek epic added $6.5 million domestically on Friday and is expected to pull in $23 million through the weekend. That would put the film’s North American haul at $504 million.

	Finally, in fifth was “Katseye: Wild Hearts.” The documentary, which offers a behind-the-scenes look at the global girl group, made an estimated $2.2 million on Friday from just 724 theaters. By Sunday, it’s expected to gross about $3.8 million.

schema.headline: Box Office: ‘The End of Oak Street’ Chomps on $8.1 Million, But ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Is Still No. 1 With $19 Million

title: Darren Walker Opens His Home to Friends and Anonymous Content Emmy Nominees in Celebration of ‘Joy, Reflection, Delight and Awe’
description: Darren Walker may be new to Los Angeles as he takes the helm of Anonymous Content as president and CEO, but he’s had long relationships with key pla
body:
Darren Walker may be new to Los Angeles as he takes the helm of Anonymous Content as president and CEO, but he’s had long relationships with key players in town for years, given his distinguished career in philanthropy and nonprofits. 

	Sally Field is one of those people. So Walker was excited to learn when he took the role at Anonymous Content at the start of this year that Field was a client. And Field was there on Wednesday evening to cheer on her friend as Walker toasted Anonymous Content’s Emmy nominees this year and showed off his famous new digs at a historic Los Angeles address.
	

	Walker delighted the intimate crowd of a few dozen friends and associates with the kismet story of how he came to purchase the sui generis, 4,400-square foot property designed as the personal residence of legendary Los Angeles architect Paul Revere Williams. 


	Much of the home is outfitted with original fixtures and an array of bespoke touches that the renowned architect handcrafted for his family residence. The home is in a historic neighborhood that reflected post-World War II Los Angeles’ embrace of mid-century modern building design and mid-century, West Coast modern attitudes about race, class and equality. 

	Of all the intricate and meticulously designed touches that Walker pointed out in the home, the one that generated the most oohs and ahhs was the lovingly built, extra-large vanity that Williams built into one wall for his wife, Della Mae Williams. At one point it was complete with giant, helmet-style hair dryers and salon-style chairs, but sadly those were gutted by a previous owner, Walker explained. Della Mae’s home beauty salon — big enough for her to invite a few friends — was but one example of how Williams was determined to present his wife with “every one of the beautiful luxuries that he built into the homes of the wealthiest families in Beverly Hills and Brentwood,” Walker said.
	



	

					Emmy nominees Matthew Rhys, Kate O’Flynn, Sally Field, Sarah Pidgeon and Sonja Warfield flank Anonymous Content chief Darren Walker at the Anonymous Content Emmy Party held Aug. 12 at Walker’s home in Los Angeles. (Todd Williamson / JanuaryImages)
									Todd Williamson/JanuaryImages for Anonymous Content
	



	Walker’s rise to national prominence and influence in philanthropy during his run atop of the Ford Foundation mirrors Williams’ ascent in his field. Walker made the 90-degree turn to lead a talent management firm active in content development came at the behest of his longtime friend Laurene Powell Jobs, whose Emerson Collective owns Anonymous Content. 

	Walker’s enthusiasm for his new job was evident in his neatly arranged, oh-so-classic Mid-City Los Angeles backyard as he introduced Anonymous Content’s Emmy nominees in attendance one by one: Sally Field (for her star turn in the Netflix film “Remarkably Bright Creatures”; Kate O’Flynn (“Widow’s Bay”), Sarah Pidgeon (“Love Story: John F Kennedy Jr. and Carolyn Bessette,”) Matthew Rhys (“The Beast in Me,” “Widow’s Bay”), Sonja Warfield (“The Gilded Age”).

	“I’m delighted to welcome you to this celebration at a time when we need moments for inspiration and joy, reflection, delight and awe and to recognize excellence more than ever,” Walker told the crowd. 

	Among those lending an ear and munching on light appetizers were Ava DuVernay, Thomas Doherty, Andy Parker, Kal Penn, Rich Appel, Keith Cox, Dee Johnson, Sophie de Bruijn, Jeremy Barber, Jiao Chen, Michael Dinner, LACMA’s Michael Govan, Jeff Sharp, Dan Lin, Kevin McCormick, Courtenay Miles, Lisa Taback, Matt Tyrnauer, Bryan Unkeless and Talitha Watkins.

	(Pictured top: Darren Walker with Emmy nominee Sarah Pidgeon)

title: Selena Gomez's Attorney Calls Fraud Accusations 'Meritless'
description:
Selena Gomez
                          Fraud Claims Are Totally Bogus, Lawyer Says
body:
Selena Gomez
                          Fraud Claims Are Totally Bogus, Lawyer Says
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 15, 2026
                            12:08 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Selena Gomez's lawyer says the claims against his client are total BS ... and they're ready to fight it out in court.
      
    
            Matthew Rosengart released a statement after two companies filed a lawsuit against Selena, her mother, Mandy Teefey, and their former business partner, Daniella Pierson, claiming they misrepresented the strength of their mental health company, Wondermind, to investors.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            He tells TMZ ... allegations against Selena engaged in any fraud or other wrongdoing are "completely meritless, both factually and legally." PEOPLE was the first to report Rosengart's statement.
      

            Rosengart promises to vigorously defend his client from the allegations ... and adds he's already working on a motion to dismiss the "baseless claims."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As we reported ... Wondermind SRS 44 LLC and Bespoke Wondermind LLC are suing the three women over Wondermind Global -- claiming they made false representations about the infrastructure, leadership and resources necessary for the company to launch into a profitable platform.
      
    
            Despite appearing in multiple interviews about the company, Wondermind SRS 44 LLC and Bespoke Wondermind LLC say Selena was barely involved with the actual operations ... and they allege Daniella stretched the truth about her success in the business world.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The companies claim "for three years, while the company quietly collapsed around them, not one of its founders, officers or directors said a word to the investors whose money was funding the collapse.” They say they only learned of the company's issues because of an article published by The Cut -- which also alleged Mandy had substance abuse issues.
      
    
            Mandy denied the substance abuse claims and that the company was a mess to The Cut.

                          Sues Landlord Over $17k a Month Rental Claiming Pest and Plumbing Issues

            Da’Vine Joy Randolph is dragging her landlord to court … claiming she rented a luxury home for $17K a month … only to have to deal with pests and plumbing issues ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            The Oscar-winning actress is suing a leasing company, 421 NRD LLC, claiming its $5+ million rental turned into a nightmare with a whole host of problems.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Da’Vine said she leased a high-end 5-bedroom, 6-bathroom, 4,452-square-foot home in Los Angeles for $17,000 per month in September 2024.
      

            She said the company promised the home was in good condition ... but says she moved in and had to deal with water issues, pest conditions, door and window failures, defective locks, plumbing conditions, inconsistent water pressure, and safety concerns.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Da’Vine claims that when she raised the issues, the landlord made insufficient fixes and eventually told her she could move out if she was unhappy.
      
    
            The actress is suing for breach of the lease and bunch of other things.  She's seeking unspecified damages and wants to be reimbursed for her out-of-pocket expenses like hotels she had to stay in during repairs and pest control.
